property_summary: For any new owner address supplied to transferOwnership by the current owner, the contract's owner getter must equal that supplied address after the call; the mutant sets owner to address(0) and thus violates this for any _newOwner != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner must equal the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead leaves owner unchanged (still msg.sender) and thus violates that rule for inputs where newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller who is the current owner and any proposed newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead leaves owner as the caller, violating this when newOwner != msg.sender.

For any owner caller and any proposed newOwner address (possibly equal), when transferOwnership(newOwner) is called by the current owner, the contract's owner() becomes exactly newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead leaves owner as the caller when newOwner != msg.sender, breaking this rule.

For any address caller who is the current owner and any proposed newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in the contract's owner() equaling newOwner (i.e., owner is set to the provided newOwner); the mutant that writes owner = msg.sender instead leaves owner as the caller whenever newOwner != msg.sender, violating this rule.

For any address newOwner and any owner caller, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() becomes exactly newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead leaves owner as the caller when newOwner != msg.sender, violating this rule.

Invariant: only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership (so after any transferOwnership attempt, the owner is either unchanged or updated only when msg.sender was the previous owner); the mutant inverts the guard so non-owners can call it and thus changes owner when called by non-owners, violating this rule.

For any caller address X and any newOwner address Y, when X is the contract's current owner, calling transferOwnership(Y) must result in owner == Y; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner check allows non-owner callers to change owner, so there exist X,Y where this property is violated (a non-owner X can set owner to Y).

Invariant: calling transferOwnership from the current owner always succeeds and updates owner to the provided newOwner; the mutant restricts onlyOwner to owner==address(0) so non-zero owners cannot call transferOwnership and thus the invariant can be violated.

Calling owned() (which is onlyOwner) must never change the owner state; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so for some caller sequences the owner value will change in the mutant but never in the reference.

Rule: Calling owned() must never change the contract's owner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() violates this when owned() is invoked by an address different from the current owner.

For any caller, invoking owned() (a function restricted by onlyOwner) does not change C.owner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner when owned() is (improperly) invoked by a different address, so the test ensures owner remains the same after a successful call to owned().

For any caller who is the current owner, a successful call to owned() does not change C.owner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() will change owner when owned() is invoked by a caller that is the owner but different from the stored owner (impossible), so we instead use fuzzed sequence: set owner to some address via transferOwnership (by the initial owner), then have that owner call owned() — the correct contract preserves owner, the mutant also preserves when caller==owner, so to catch mutant we must instead detect that owned() should be callable only by owner (i.e., a non-owner call reverts) — the mutant still keeps onlyOwner but mutates state only when owner calls; however, a distinguishing universal property is: after deployment owner is address(this)??

For any address actor, if actor is NOT the current owner then calling owned() must revert (onlyOwner); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() still has the onlyOwner modifier, so to distinguish we instead use a sequence: ensure a fuzzed address newOwner is set via transferOwnership by the rightful owner, then when newOwner calls owned() it must NOT change the owner — the reference keeps owner equal to newOwner after the call, while the mutant will also keep it if caller==owner, so instead we assert that a non-owner caller cannot change owner: after a non-owner attempts to call owned() the contract's owner must remain the same (and the call must revert).

For all callers, invoking owned() does not change the contract's owner: only the current owner can perform owner-only actions, so owner() remains equal to the pre-call owner; the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to call owned() and potentially change owner, violating this invariant for some caller address.

For any caller address, calling owned() must not change the contract's owner: owner() remains equal to the pre-call owner for all callers in the correct contract; the mutant that removes the onlyOwner require allows a non-owner caller to call owned() and (if owned() mutates owner) can change owner(), violating this invariant for some caller addresses.

For any caller address, invoking owned() does not change C.owner() — in the correct contract only the current owner can call owner-only functions so owner() remains unchanged for all callers; the mutant removes the require allowing a non-owner caller to call owned() and (if owned() mutates owner) can change owner(), violating this invariant for some fuzzed caller addresses.
